reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts the most recent AI use figure for Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, at 15.0%, against 13.7% in the prior period. The question behind that number is narrow and behavioral: in the last two weeks, did this business use AI. The series has asked it since September 2023, and the Census Bureau suppresses figures where the sample will not support them. The important caveat for a nonprofit reader is that this is not a nonprofit-specific measurement. It is the closest official proxy the survey offers, and it covers a category broader than the sector itself.

What the sector actually does with AI is described by the Center for Effective Philanthropy, whose sector research, including its AI-focused reporting, examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, tracks the funding side, including grantmaking trends and funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure. The World of AI's own coverage of this sector frames the practical territory as grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets, with governance capacity as the constraint. Those three uses, back-office writing and analysis, donor-facing analytics, and program delivery, are where the material places deployment.

Candid also describes a demand-side shift that matters more than any internal tool. Donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities, which means many will not ever see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter. That reframes AI adoption from an efficiency question into a visibility question, because the research layer where funding decisions begin is moving away from properties the organization controls.

On the supply side, The World of AI catalogues four individually verified organizations in its nonprofits and open source foundations listing, two nonprofits and two open source foundations, each with a sourced classification note. LMSYS is the most directly AI-central, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the broader AI community uses to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy is described as an end user of AI capability in education rather than a producer of it, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The same page is explicit about what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights for public use, with the notes confirming only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

The access gap is where the sector's own organizations concentrate their work. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, turning public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning environments and bringing senior citizens and student volunteers together to explore practical AI tools. It operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities, and runs the International AI for Impact Challenge, where top participants secure engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN, which runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption, states plainly that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector, and promotes an Equity Guide, professional certificates, scholarships, and open source tools built for nonprofit and advocacy use.

On returns and regulation the harvested material is largely silent, and it is worth saying so rather than filling the gap. No source here reports a measured ROI figure for nonprofit AI deployment, and none sets out a regulatory posture specific to the sector. Stanford HAI's AI Index is cited as the annual macro series reporting AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations, which is where a reader would look for that evidence, but no figures from it appear in this material. The nearest thing to a risk finding is Candid's observation about donors researching charities through AI tools rather than through the charity's own channels.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a modest reading. Adoption in the closest measured category sits at 15.0%, so this is not a sector that has already moved, and the constraint the coverage names is governance capacity rather than tooling. The uses with the clearest description are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets, and the funding side is tracked by Candid while the equity and skills side is addressed by the AI Equity Project and NTEN. The strategic risk the sources do identify is disintermediation at the donor research stage, which is a communications and discoverability problem as much as a technology one.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four individually verified organisations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, each with a sourced classification note. It states that LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a neutral evaluation platform, while Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education, and the Krita and Blender Foundations steward creative software tools. The notes confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. The page also notes the list excludes training compute providers, standards bodies, and open-model foundations that release weights.
